shelf_items.name: Richard Thaler and Werner De Bondt (1985) - Overreaction Hypothesis
shelf_items.what_it_found: Stocks that performed poorly over 3-5 years (losers) subsequently outperformed past winners by about 25% over the next 3-5 years, contradicting market efficiency.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Empirical study using NYSE data; replicated many times; foundational for behavioral finance.
shelf_items.why_buried: EMH proponents dismissed it as data mining or risk-based; Thaler's work was initially rejected by top journals.
shelf_items.current_status: Now widely accepted as a robust anomaly; forms basis for contrarian strategies.

shelf_items.name: Robert Shiller (1981) - Excess Volatility
shelf_items.what_it_found: Stock market volatility is far higher than can be justified by changes in dividends, implying irrational pricing.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Statistical analysis of S&P 500 data; replicated; won Nobel Prize.
shelf_items.why_buried: EMH advocates like Eugene Fama argued volatility could be explained by time-varying discount rates.
shelf_items.current_status: Now a cornerstone of behavioral finance; Shiller's CAPE ratio widely used.

shelf_items.name: Narasimhan Jegadeesh and Sheridan Titman (1993) - Momentum Strategy
shelf_items.what_it_found: Buying past 6-month winners and selling losers yields 1% per month over next 6 months, contradicting weak-form EMH.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Robust empirical finding; replicated across markets and time periods.
shelf_items.why_buried: EMH predicted no predictability; initially met with skepticism; later accepted as anomaly.
shelf_items.current_status: Momentum is now a standard factor in asset pricing models (e.g., Fama-French-Carhart).

shelf_items.name: Benoit Mandelbrot (1963) - Fractal Markets Hypothesis
shelf_items.what_it_found: Price changes follow stable Paretian distributions with infinite variance, not normal; markets exhibit long memory and self-similarity.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Empirical analysis of cotton prices; later confirmed in many assets.
shelf_items.why_buried: EMH relied on normal distributions; Mandelbrot's work was mathematically complex and dismissed as exotic.
shelf_items.current_status: Rediscovered in econophysics; still marginalized in mainstream finance.

shelf_items.name: George Soros (1987) - Reflexivity Theory
shelf_items.what_it_found: Market prices can influence fundamentals, creating feedback loops that lead to bubbles and crashes, contradicting EMH's rational expectations.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Case studies (e.g., 1987 crash); Soros's trading success; limited academic formalization.
shelf_items.why_buried: Dismissed as anecdotal; not mathematically rigorous; EMH framework had no room for reflexivity.
shelf_items.current_status: Gaining traction in behavioral finance and complexity economics; still not mainstream.

shelf_items.name: Andrew Lo (2004) - Adaptive Markets Hypothesis
shelf_items.what_it_found: Markets are not always efficient; efficiency is context-dependent and evolves with market participants' behavior and environment.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Theoretical framework with empirical support from behavioral and evolutionary finance.
shelf_items.why_buried: Challenged the universal validity of EMH; initially met with resistance from efficient market proponents.
shelf_items.current_status: Growing acceptance as a middle ground between EMH and behavioral finance.
